exhibits.title: Mechanical calculating machines 1900-70
exhibits.body: Mechanical calculating machines Commerce and industry expanded rapidly in the 18th and 19th centuries. Huge amounts of money flowed around the world's economy and it all needed to be totted up, banked and recorded. To help meet this demand for mass calculation, powerful desktop calculating machines were installed in banks, factories, offices and shops to keep track of money. Vast numbers of calculators like the ones on show were in use by the early 20th century, but they were difficult to operate and required extensive training. Operators often sat in long rows amid deafening noise as they worked at identical machines. Object numbers and sources are listed in the large-print books at the ends of the gallery. *With his Burroughs, Mr Nickles knows, each day, his sales, costs and profits. exhibits.body: Calculating machine A out This is one of the earliest mechanical caiculating machines in Britain. It was invented in 1666 by the mathematician Samuel Morland for counting money quickly and accurately. The machine has individual dials for farthings. pence and shillings, as well as for pounds, from units to tens of thousands. A stylus rotated the dials - clockwise for addition, anticlockwise for subtraction. Counters kept track of totals. Several were made, one being shown to the diarist Samuel Pepys. He described it as 'very pretty. but not very useful: Donated by: Major-General H P Babbage Object no: 1905-109

exhibits.title: Global postioning system (GPS) receiver 1993
exhibits.body: Global postioning system (GPS) receiver Navigation remains a mathematical praction, although the technologies change over time. Today, GPS satelites orbiting the Earth broadcast time signals from on-board clocks, Our GPS receivers calculate our position by measuring tiny time differences between the signals. This is done using a technique known as trilateration, involving the geometry of circles and triangles. However, GPS signals are weak and can be delberately jammed. Some navigation specialists worry that people wil have lost the ablity to navigate if the system falls. Older methods are being reintroduced as backups.

How likely was it that a face seen in a camera matched face patterns stored in the machine's memory? Artificial neural networks learn from their surroundings using the mathematics of probability. exhibits.title: In 1950, Alan Turing, now famed for code-
exhibits.body: In 1950, Alan Turing, now famed for code- breaking during the Second World War, asked the question 'Can machines think?' Three decades later, the machine to your left debuted on national television. It seemed the answer might soon be 'yes. A critical sign of intelligence is recognising patterns. The machine had first been trained with pictures of its creators' faces. Then, one after another, the scientists sat in front of a live camera linked to the machine. It had to decide whether any of the faces it saw matched the face patterns stored in its memory. It recognised them all, calling out each scientist's name. Then a scientist new to the machine walked in. 'INTRUDER! INTRUDER!' it shouted. *The computer immediately spots the odd man out, the television presenter said. The security implications are obvious

exhibits.title: Trigonometry instrument 1664
exhibits.body: Trigonometry instrument This machine was used to simplify calculations involving triangles, using a mathematical technique known as trigonometry. Surveyors rely extensively on this practice as it enables huge areas to be surveyed using the lengths and angles of triangles. The operator used the machine by drawing the problem on it. It contained three rules which could be moved using dials to make a triangle of the required size. Angles or lengths could then be read off directly. However, it was expensive and did not catch on. Then he usec te matematica teennique showilds harmonic analysis to break down the complicated tidal motion into a series of simpler components. Finally, he used this machine to recombine them for future tides. Cranking the handle for tour hours gave him tidal predictions for one year. exhibits.title: London Hospital Survival Predictor About 1972
exhibits.body: London Hospital Survival Predictor About 1972 Difficult decisions about probability and risk are made by hospital medical staff day in, day out. At the London Hospital in Whitechapel medics needed to decide the likelihood of patients in comas making recoveries. This machine was built to help their diagnosis. It compared brain measurements from the coma patient with those from previous patients, stored in the machine's memory. The needle would then point somewhere between the letter S, meaning "survive, and IBD, meaning irreversible brain damage. Nevertheless, the final decision about resuscitation was always made by doctors. Donated by: St Bartholomew's Hospital

exhibits.body: 10 11 Time-telling and surveying. 1552-1725 Hand-held quadrants were long-established and familiar mathematical tools, a common sight in London's instrument-making workshops. There were different types for different uses. Horary quadrants were used for Time-telling, altitude quadrants for simple surveying tasks and Gunter quadrants for basic astronomical calculation including time-tetling. They were available in assorted materials and sizes, and provided an affordable alternative to buying a set of expensive instruments. exhibits.title: 11 Isaac Newton's Principia, 1687
exhibits.body: 11 Isaac Newton's Principia, 1687 Newton is perhaps most famous for the principles laid out in his book Principia - concepts now known as theoretical physics. To account for the motion of planets, moons and comets within the Solar System. he set out his three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation. He showed how objects here on Earth and in space follow the same natural laws, which can be expressed mathematically. Facsimile cover page. Written by Isaac Newton, published in London Science Museum Group

exhibits.title: 12 Isaac Newton's Opticks, 1704
exhibits.body: 12 Isaac Newton's Opticks, 1704 Newton began his experiments with light and lenses in the 1660s. While experimenting he discovered that white light consisted of a spectrum of different colours. He maintained a long-term interest in the theory of light. He announced his dramatic findings in correspondence to the Royal Society in 1672 and the first edition of his authoritative account of the science of light, Opticks, appeared in 1704. Written by Isaac Newton, published in London Science Museum Group

exhibits.title: Dividing engine for making scales on instruments, late 1700s, modified 1800s
exhibits.body: Dividing engine for making scales on instruments, late 1700s, modified 1800s Dividing engines partially mechanised the process of dividing scales for small instruments, helping to meet growing demand from navigators. A sextant or octant was fixed to the top of the engine, and angular divisions were marked on it using the engine's precision screw and a ratchet. Jesse Ramsden constructed the first such engine in London, reluctantly sharing its design with other makers at the request of the government's Board of Longitude. exhibits.body: Octant made using a dividing engine, about 1800 Octants were inexpensive navigation instruments used well into the 1800s. This octant carries a small faint mark in the centre of its scale, showing an anchor and the initials EP: These marks were applied to instruments made using the dividing engine of Edward Pritchard. exhibits.title: Portrait of Jesse Ramsden, about 1790
exhibits.body: Portrait of Jesse Ramsden, about 1790 This portrait of Jesse Ramsden portrays an instrument- maker at the height of his talent and popularity. Towering in the background is a large astronomical circle made for Palermo Observatory, one of Ramsden's many commissions for European customers. By his side is a dividing engine. his invention that enabled the fast and accurate division of scales on small instruments for navigation and surveying. Painted by Robert Home, probably in London Lent by the Royal Society. Object no. L2018-507

exhibits.title: Jesse Ramsden (1735-1800)
exhibits.body: Lent by the Royal Society: Object no. L2018-507 Jesse Ramsden (1735-1800) Jesse Ramsden was London's leading maker of mathematical instruments in the late 1700s. Born in. Halifax in Yorkshire, he began his apprenticeship in London at the late age of 21. His products were praised for their precision and quality. Ramsden was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society and awarded the coveted Copley Medal in 1795 for his various inventions and improvements to philosophical instruments'.

This globe was sold by Messrs. Puttick and Simpson... on July 8th 1890. Actually made in1828 by Qi Mei-lu in Wuyuan Province. It was inspired by the publication of Gao-hou Meng-qui published Shanghai, 1807. The stand reflects that of Verbiest's six foot diameter celestial globe at the Imperial Observatory, Peking.
